title: GitHub Personal
subtitle: Dedicated profile for personal GitHub repositories

steps: Copy your public key using the Copy button above.
Open GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key.
Set Title to "{host_pattern}" and Key type to "Authentication Key".
Paste your public key into the Key field and click "Add SSH key".
Test your connection using the Test Connection button below.
warnings: If you have multiple GitHub accounts, update existing repo remotes: git remote set-url origin git@{host_pattern}:org/repo.git
If GitHub says 'Key is already in use', this public key is already tied to another account. Generate a new dedicated key with a unique name.

title: GitHub Work / Organization
subtitle: Separate work organization repos with an isolated key

steps: Copy your public key using the Copy button above.
Open GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key.
Set Title to "{host_pattern}" and Key type to "Authentication Key".
Paste your public key into the Key box and click "Add SSH key".
If your organization enforces SAML SSO, click 'Configure SSO' next to the key and click 'Authorize'.
Test authentication using the Test Connection button below.
warnings: Organization SSO Notice: Remember to click 'Configure SSO' → 'Authorize' for your organization after adding the key.
Clone your work repositories with: git clone git@{host_pattern}:org/repo.git

title: GitLab Profile
subtitle: GitLab.com or self-hosted enterprise GitLab instance

steps: Copy your public key using the Copy button above.
Open GitLab → User Settings → SSH Keys (or click the direct link above).
Paste the key into the Key field, set Title to "{host_pattern}", and set optional expiration.
Click "Add key".
Test connection using the Test Connection button below.
warnings: For self-hosted GitLab instances, open your instance's User Settings → SSH Keys page instead.

title: AWS EC2 / Lightsail
subtitle: Amazon Linux / Ubuntu EC2 instance with 60s keepalive

steps: Copy your public key or use the 1-click ssh-copy-id tool below.
Verify your EC2 Security Group permits inbound SSH on port {port} from your IP.
Ensure the public key is appended to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the instance.
Connect in terminal using: ssh {host_pattern}
warnings: Default usernames for AWS: Ubuntu ('ubuntu'), Amazon Linux 2023 ('ec2-user'), Debian ('admin'), CentOS ('centos').
If ssh-copy-id fails with syntax errors, use the Troubleshooting panel below.

title: Hetzner Cloud VPS
subtitle: Fast European cloud server with root or sudo user

steps: Copy your public key or install it with the 1-click ssh-copy-id button below.
Or add this key to Hetzner Cloud Console → Security → SSH Keys to auto-provision on new servers.
Connect with: ssh {host_pattern}
warnings: If connecting as root, ensure PermitRootLogin is allowed in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.

steps: Copy your public key or install it with 1-click ssh-copy-id.
You can also register this key in DigitalOcean Settings → Security → SSH Keys for auto-injection in new Droplets.
Connect with: ssh {host_pattern}
warnings: Droplets initially deployed with password auth require ssh-copy-id or manual key copy before passwordless login works.

title: Bastion / Jump Host
subtitle: Securely route traffic to an internal host via Jump server

steps: Ensure your SSH key is authorized on BOTH the bastion ({proxy_jump}) AND the target host ({host_name}).
Step 1: Install key to bastion: ssh-copy-id {proxy_jump}
Step 2: Install key to target: ssh-copy-id -o ProxyJump={proxy_jump} {host_pattern}
Connect transparently: ssh {host_pattern}
warnings: Dual-Key Requirement: The intermediate bastion and the target private host each verify SSH keys independently.
ForwardAgent Security: If ForwardAgent is enabled, your private key agent is forwarded to the bastion. Only use this with trusted jump hosts.

title: Raspberry Pi / Homelab
subtitle: Home server, Raspberry Pi, or local Linux machine

steps: Copy your public key or use the 1-click ssh-copy-id tool below.
Install key to Pi: ssh-copy-id {user}@{host_name}
Verify local mDNS resolution: ensure '{host_name}' resolves on your local network.
Connect with: ssh {host_pattern}
warnings: If raspberrypi.local fails to resolve, replace HostName with the static LAN IP (e.g. 192.168.1.50).

config.notes: Access remote Postgres locally at localhost:5432

steps: Ensure your SSH key is authorized on the gateway server ({host_name}).
Open the tunnel in background: ssh -N {host_pattern}
Connect your local database client (e.g. pgAdmin, DBeaver, psql) to: 127.0.0.1:5432
Keep the SSH connection alive while querying the database.
warnings: The tunnel terminates when the SSH process closes. Use 'ssh -N' to keep it active without an interactive shell.
Ensure local port 5432 is not already in use by a local PostgreSQL service.

title: MySQL / Redis Tunnel
subtitle: Forward remote MySQL (3306) or Redis (6379) to local

config.notes: Access remote MySQL locally at localhost:3306

steps: Ensure your SSH key is authorized on the gateway server ({host_name}).
Open the tunnel: ssh -N {host_pattern}
Connect your local MySQL client / TablePlus / DBeaver to: 127.0.0.1:3306
Keep the SSH connection alive while using the database.
warnings: Use 'ssh -N' (no remote command) to keep the port tunnel open in the background.
